Twenty-four mammals, and what it would take to keep them.

Across six regions, 10 of these species are critically endangered, the last step before extinction in the wild. 5 others have moved to a safer category, proof that protection works.

How the Red List ranks risk

The IUCN Red List places each species on one scale, from safe to gone. The three categories in the middle count as threatened.

  1. LCLeast ConcernWidespread and not at risk for now.
  2. NTNear ThreatenedClose to qualifying as threatened.
  3. VUVulnerableHigh risk of extinction in the wild.
  4. ENEndangeredVery high risk of extinction in the wild.
  5. CRCritically EndangeredExtremely high risk of extinction in the wild.
  6. EWExtinct in the WildSurvives only in captivity.
  7. EXExtinctNo individuals remain.

Countries keep their own lists too. A species can be stable worldwide and still endangered in one place, like the koala in eastern Australia or the Canada lynx in the lower 48 US states.

Conservation works

Five animals in this guide have moved to a safer category after decades of protection. None of them recovered on their own.

What you can do

Most of the work happens far from here, through groups that protect habitat and run breeding programs. You can back them.

  1. Look a species up

    The Red List publishes the current assessment for every species, with its range and threats.

    Search the IUCN Red List

  2. Support field work

    Donations to established groups pay for rangers, habitat protection and anti-poaching patrols.

    World Wildlife Fund

  3. Visit an accredited zoo

    Accredited zoos run many of the breeding programs behind the comebacks, including the black-footed ferret and red wolf.

    Find an AZA zoo
